title: Binary Search
description: You are given a list of numbers that is already sorted from smallest to largest, and one 'target' number to find. Your job is to return the position (index) of that number in the list. If the number is not in the list, return -1.

examples.explanation: Start checking the middle of the list. Since 9 is bigger than the middle values, keep narrowing to the right side. Eventually you land on index 4, where the value is 9.
As you narrow the search, you will notice 2 falls between 0 and 3, but 2 itself is not present anywhere in the list. So the answer is -1.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4 (the list can have from 1 up to 10,000 numbers)
-10^4 < nums[i], target < 10^4 (all numbers, including the target, are between -10,000 and 10,000)
All the numbers in nums are unique (no duplicates)
nums is already sorted from smallest to largest
hints: Keep two pointers, left and right, marking the current search area.
Calculate mid as left + (right - left) / 2 instead of (left + right) / 2, so the numbers never get too large and cause overflow errors.
followUp: Can you write both an iterative version (using a loop) and a recursive version (using function calls)?

testCases.note: Normal case - target exists in the middle-ish of the list.
Target does not exist anywhere in the list.
Edge case - list has only one element, and it matches the target.
Edge case - list has only one element, and it does NOT match the target.
Edge case - target is the very first element of the list.

title: Search Insert Position
description: You are given a sorted list of numbers and a target number. If the target already exists in the list, return its index (position). If it does not exist, imagine inserting it into the list so the list stays sorted, and return the index where it would go.

examples.explanation: 5 is already present in the list at index 2, so we simply return that index.
2 is not in the list, but if we inserted it, it would fit right between 1 and 3, which is index 1.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4 (list has 1 to 10,000 numbers)
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4 (all numbers in the list fit in this range)
All numbers in nums are different from each other and already sorted
-10^4 <= target <= 10^4 (target is also in this range)
hints: Run a normal binary search using left <= right as your loop condition.
When the loop finishes, the value of 'left' is automatically the correct answer, whether the target was found or not.
followUp: Can you extend this idea to find both the first and last position a number could be inserted (called lower_bound and upper_bound)?

testCases.note: Normal case - target already exists in the list.
Normal case - target needs to be inserted in the middle.
Edge case - target is bigger than every number, so it goes at the very end.
Edge case - target is smaller than every number, so it goes at the very start.
Edge case - the list is empty, so the target must be inserted at index 0.

title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
description: Imagine playing a number guessing game: a number between 1 and n has been secretly picked, and you need to figure out what it is. Every time you guess, you get told 'too high', 'too low', or 'correct!' through a special guess() function. Find the number that was picked.

examples.input: n = 10, the secretly picked number is 6
examples.explanation: We start guessing around the middle of 1 to 10. Each guess tells us to go higher or lower, and we narrow down until we correctly guess 6.

examples.input: n = 1, the secretly picked number is 1
examples.explanation: There is only one possible number to pick from, so it must be 1 - no guessing needed.

constraints: 1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1 (n can be a very large number, up to about 2.1 billion)
1 <= pick <= n (the secret number is always somewhere inside the valid range)
hints: Keep a range from 1 to n, and always guess the middle of the current range.
Shrink the range to the left or right half depending on whether guess() says 'too high' or 'too low'.

youtubeVideos.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower - LeetCode 374

relatedProblems: Guess Number Higher or Lower II
followUp: How would you solve the harder version, Guess Number Higher or Lower II, where you must minimize how much money you'd lose in the worst case?

testCases.note: Normal case - number is somewhere in the middle of the range.
Edge case - only one possible number exists, so no real guessing is needed.
Edge case - the picked number is at the very start of the range.
Edge case - the picked number is at the very end of the range.
Edge case - n is at its maximum allowed value, testing that your code handles very large numbers correctly.

title: First Bad Version
description: Imagine your company released versions 1, 2, 3, ... n of a product one after another. At some point, a bug was introduced, and every version released after that point is 'bad'. You are given a function isBadVersion(version) that tells you if a version is bad or not, but calling it too many times is expensive, so you want to find the very first bad version using as few checks as possible.

examples.input: n = 5, and versions 4 and 5 are known to be bad
examples.explanation: Versions 1, 2, and 3 are good, but starting from version 4 everything is bad. So the first bad version is 4.
There's only one version total, and it happens to be bad, so it must be the first bad one.

constraints: 1 <= bad <= n <= 2^31 - 1 (n can be a very large number of versions)
hints: Binary search for the leftmost (first) position where isBadVersion returns true.
Even after finding a bad version, keep checking to the left in case an earlier version is also bad.
followUp: How would your approach change if every call to isBadVersion() was extremely slow or costly?

testCases.note: Normal case - the bad version is somewhere in the middle-to-end range.
Edge case - only one version exists, and it is the bad one.
Edge case - the very first version is already bad, meaning nothing is good.
Edge case - only the very last version is bad, all others are good.
Edge case - n is extremely large, testing that your search stays efficient (O(log n)) even at max scale.

title: Sqrt(x)
description: You are given a non-negative whole number x, and you need to find its square root, but rounded down to the nearest whole number. You are not allowed to use any built-in sqrt() or power functions - you must calculate it yourself.

examples.explanation: 2 multiplied by itself equals exactly 4, so the square root is exactly 2.
The real square root of 8 is about 2.83, but since we round down to a whole number, the answer is 2.

constraints: 0 <= x <= 2^31 - 1 (x can be 0 up to a very large number, about 2.1 billion)
hints: Binary search in the range from 0 to x, checking if mid * mid <= x.
Watch out for very large numbers - use a data type like 'long' when squaring mid so it doesn't overflow.
followUp: Can you get a more precise (decimal) answer using Newton's Method instead of binary search?

testCases.note: Normal case - x is a perfect square.
Normal case - x is not a perfect square, so the result gets rounded down.
Edge case - smallest possible input, square root of 0 is 0.
Edge case - square root of 1 is 1.
Edge case - x is at the maximum allowed value, testing that your multiplication does not overflow.

title: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix
description: You are given a grid (matrix) of numbers where each row is sorted from largest to smallest (left to right), and each column is also sorted from largest to smallest (top to bottom). Your task is to count how many numbers in the entire grid are negative.

examples.explanation: Counting every negative number across all four rows gives a total of 8 negative numbers.
There isn't a single negative number anywhere in this small grid, so the count is 0.

constraints: m == grid.length (number of rows)
n == grid[i].length (number of columns)
1 <= m, n <= 100 (the grid can be up to 100 rows and 100 columns)
-100 <= grid[i][j] <= 100 (every value in the grid is between -100 and 100)
hints: For each row, binary search for the first index where the numbers turn negative.
Add up (row length minus that index) for every row to get the total count.

youtubeVideos.title: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix - LeetCode 1351

followUp: Can you solve this even faster, in O(m + n) time, by starting from a corner of the grid and walking like a staircase?

testCases.note: Normal case - a mix of positive and negative numbers spread across the grid.
Edge case - no negative numbers at all.
Edge case - every single number in the grid is negative.
Edge case - grid has only a single cell, and it's positive.
Edge case - grid has only a single cell, and it's negative.

title: Check If N and Its Double Exist
description: You are given an array of numbers, and you need to figure out if there are two different positions i and j (not the same position) where one number is exactly double the other - meaning arr[i] equals 2 times arr[j].

examples.explanation: 5 is at one position and 10 is at another, and 10 equals 2 times 5, so the condition is satisfied.
No number in this array is exactly double another number, so the answer is false.

constraints: 2 <= arr.length <= 500 (the array has between 2 and 500 numbers)
-1000 <= arr[i] <= 1000 (every number is between -1000 and 1000)
hints: Sort the array first, then binary search for either double or half of each element.
Handle the zero case separately: you need at least two zeros in the array for it to count.

youtubeVideos.title: Check If N and Its Double Exist - LeetCode 1346

followUp: Can you solve this in a single O(n) pass using a HashSet instead of sorting?

testCases.note: Normal case - 10 is double of 5.
Normal case - no pair satisfies the double condition.
Edge case - two zeros count as valid since 2 * 0 = 0.
Edge case - a single zero has no valid partner, so this is false.
Edge case - negative numbers are also valid; -20 is double of -10.

title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
description: A 'mountain array' is a list of numbers that first keeps increasing, reaches one highest point (the peak), and then keeps decreasing - just like walking up and then down a mountain. Your task is to find the index of that peak (highest point).

examples.explanation: The array rises from 0 to 1 and then falls back to 0, so the peak (highest point) is at index 1, where the value is 1.
The values rise from 0 up to 2 and then fall down to 1 and then 0, so the peak is at index 1, where the value is 2.

constraints: 3 <= arr.length <= 10^5 (the array has at least 3 numbers, since a mountain needs an up-slope, a peak, and a down-slope)
0 <= arr[i] <= 10^6 (every value is between 0 and 1,000,000)
The array is guaranteed to always be a valid mountain shape
hints: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1] to figure out if you are on the rising side or the falling side of the mountain.
You never need to compare arr[mid] with arr[mid - 1] separately.

youtubeVideos.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array - NeetCode

followUp: What would you need to change if the mountain could have multiple equally-high peaks?

testCases.note: Edge case - smallest possible mountain array with just 3 elements.
Normal case - peak is close to the start of the array.
Normal case - peak is roughly in the middle of a longer array.
Edge case - peak is at the very last index (mountain only rises, then drops off at the end).
Edge case - peak is at the very first index (mountain starts at its highest point).

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description: You are given a list of numbers already sorted from smallest to largest, along with a target sum. Find two different numbers in the list that add up exactly to the target, and return their positions (1-indexed, meaning the first position is numbered 1, not 0).

examples.explanation: The numbers at positions 1 and 2 (values 2 and 7) add up to 9, so we return their 1-indexed positions.
The numbers at positions 1 and 3 (values 2 and 4) add up to 6.

constraints: 2 <= numbers.length <= 3 * 10^4 (the list has between 2 and 30,000 numbers)
-1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000 (every number is between -1000 and 1000)
numbers is already sorted from smallest to largest
There is guaranteed to be exactly one valid pair of numbers that works
hints: Use two pointers starting from both ends of the array and move them inward based on the current sum.
Alternatively, for each number, binary search for its needed partner (target minus that number).
followUp: Can you solve it using binary search for each element instead of the two-pointer technique?

testCases.note: Normal case - the two matching numbers are next to each other.
Normal case - the two matching numbers are at opposite ends.
Edge case - smallest possible array (only 2 elements), and it includes negative numbers.
Edge case - matching pair includes a negative number and a positive number.
Edge case - the array contains duplicate values (two 4's), testing that you still return the correct pair.

title: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target
description: You are given a sorted list of lowercase letters and one target letter. You need to find the smallest letter in the list that comes strictly after the target letter alphabetically. If every letter in the list is smaller than or equal to the target, you 'wrap around' back to the beginning and return the very first letter instead.

examples.explanation: Since 'a' comes before every letter in the list, the smallest letter that is still greater than 'a' is 'c', the very first letter.
No letter in the list is greater than 'j' (it's the biggest one there), so we wrap around and return the first letter, 'c'.

constraints: 2 <= letters.length <= 10^4 (list has between 2 and 10,000 letters)
Every letter is a lowercase English letter (a-z)
letters is sorted from smallest to largest
letters contains at least two different letters (not all the same)
target is a single lowercase English letter
hints: Use binary search to find the first letter strictly greater than the target (this is called 'upper_bound').
If your final answer index reaches past the end of the list, use index % length to wrap back to the start.

youtubeVideos.title: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target - LeetCode 744

followUp: How would you adapt this same logic to instead find the largest letter smaller than the target?

testCases.note: Edge case - target is smaller than every letter in the list.
Edge case - target equals the largest letter, so the answer wraps around to the first letter.
Normal case - target falls in between two letters in the list.
Edge case - list has many repeated letters equal to the target; answer must skip past all of them.
Edge case - target is larger than every letter, wraps all the way back to the first letter.

title: Valid Perfect Square
description: You are given a positive whole number, and you need to determine whether it is a 'perfect square'. You cannot use any built-in square root function.

examples.explanation: 4 multiplied by itself equals exactly 16, so 16 is a perfect square.
There is no whole number that, when multiplied by itself, equals exactly 14, so it is not a perfect square.

constraints: 1 <= num <= 2^31 - 1 (num can be as large as about 2.1 billion)
hints: Binary search in the range from 1 to num, looking for a mid value where mid * mid exactly equals num.
Use a data type like 'long' when squaring mid, to avoid overflow issues with very large numbers.
followUp: Can you solve this using only repeated addition, without any multiplication at all?

testCases.note: Normal case - a clear perfect square.
Normal case - a number that is not a perfect square.
Edge case - smallest possible input; 1 x 1 = 1, so it's a perfect square.
Edge case - a very large perfect square (46340 x 46340), testing that your code avoids overflow.
Edge case - the maximum allowed value, which is not a perfect square, testing boundary handling.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Imagine you had a sorted list of numbers, but then someone picked a random spot and 'rotated' it, moving the front chunk to the back (for example, [1,2,3,4,5] rotated becomes something like [3,4,5,1,2]). Your job is to find the smallest number in this rotated list.

examples.explanation: This array is the original [1,2,3,4,5] rotated so that [3,4,5] moved to the front. The smallest value is 1.
The array was rotated, but the smallest value is still easy to spot once you scan: it's 0.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000 (list has 1 to 5000 numbers)
All numbers in nums are different (no duplicates)
nums is a sorted array that has been rotated between 1 and n times
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[right] to decide which half definitely contains the minimum.
If nums[mid] is greater than nums[right], the minimum must be to the right of mid.

youtubeVideos.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array - NeetCode

relatedProblems: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
followUp: What would change in your solution if the array could contain duplicate numbers?

testCases.note: Normal case - array rotated somewhere in the middle.
Normal case - larger array with the minimum near the middle.
Edge case - array was 'rotated' 0 times, so it's still fully sorted.
Edge case - only one number in the array, so it's automatically the minimum.
Edge case - smallest possible rotated array with 2 elements.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: You are given a sorted array that has been 'rotated' at some unknown point (a chunk from the front was moved to the back), and you need to find the index of a target value. Return -1 if it's not found.

examples.explanation: Even though the array is rotated, we can still binary search it. The value 0 is found at index 4.
3 simply does not exist anywhere in this array, so we return -1.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000 (list has 1 to 5000 numbers)
All values in nums are different from each other
nums was originally sorted in ascending order, then possibly rotated
hints: At each middle point, determine which half (left or right) is still properly sorted.
Check whether the target falls within that sorted half's value range before deciding which side to search next.

youtubeVideos.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array - NeetCode

relatedProblems: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
followUp: How would your solution need to change if the array contained duplicate values?

testCases.note: Normal case - target exists in the rotated portion of the array.
Normal case - target does not exist anywhere.
Edge case - array has only a single element that matches the target.
Edge case - array has only a single element that does not match the target.
Edge case - small rotated array, target is the very first element.

title: Find Peak Element
description: A 'peak' is any number in the array that is strictly bigger than both of its neighbors. You are given an array where no two neighboring numbers are ever equal, and you need to find the index of any peak (there can be more than one, and you only need to return one of them).

examples.explanation: The value 3 at index 2 is bigger than both of its neighbors (2 and 1), so index 2 is a peak.
There are actually two valid peaks here: index 1 (value 2) and index 5 (value 6). Either answer would be accepted; index 5 is shown here.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000 (array has 1 to 1000 numbers)
-2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1 (numbers can be very large or very small)
No two neighboring numbers in the array are ever equal to each other
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1] to decide which side is guaranteed to contain a peak.
Treat anything outside the array's boundaries as if it were negative infinity, to simplify edge cases.
relatedProblems: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
followUp: Can you extend this same idea to find a peak in a 2D grid instead of a 1D array?

testCases.note: Normal case - one clear peak in the middle of the array.
Normal case - multiple valid peaks exist; any correct one is accepted.
Edge case - array has only one element, so it is automatically a peak.
Edge case - array is strictly increasing, so the peak is the last element.
Edge case - array is strictly decreasing, so the peak is the first element.

title: Time-Based Key-Value Store
description: You need to design a special storage system that remembers a value along with the exact timestamp it was saved, for any given key. Later, when someone asks for a value at a specific timestamp, you should return the most recent value that was saved at or before that timestamp - not necessarily an exact timestamp match.

examples.input: set("foo","bar",1); get("foo",1); get("foo",3); set("foo","bar2",4); get("foo",4); get("foo",5)
examples.explanation: At timestamp 1, we save 'bar'. Asking for timestamp 3 still returns 'bar' since that's the latest value at or before time 3. After saving 'bar2' at time 4, asking for time 4 or 5 both return 'bar2', since it's the newest matching value.
We save '100' starting at timestamp 2. But asking for timestamp 1, which is BEFORE anything was ever saved, returns an empty string, since there's no valid value yet at that point in time.

constraints: 1 <= key.length, value.length <= 100 (keys and values are short strings)
key and value only contain lowercase English letters and digits
1 <= timestamp <= 10^7 (timestamps can be fairly large numbers)
For the same key, every timestamp used with set() is strictly increasing (never repeated or out of order)
At most 2 * 10^5 total calls to set and get combined
hints: For each key, store a list of (timestamp, value) pairs in the order they were added - they'll naturally stay sorted by timestamp.
For get(), binary search this list for the largest timestamp that is still less than or equal to the requested timestamp.
followUp: How would you support deleting old timestamps from memory to save space over time?

testCases.note: Normal case - exact timestamp match.
Normal case - requested timestamp is after the stored one, so the stored value still applies.
Edge case - asking for a key that was never set at all, should return an empty string.
Edge case - requested timestamp falls between two saved timestamps, should return the earlier (still valid) value.
Edge case - only one value ever stored for this key, and the timestamp matches exactly.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
description: Koko the monkey has several piles of bananas and h hours to eat them all before the guards come back. She picks one eating speed k (bananas per hour) and sticks with it: in each hour, she picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer than k, she finishes that pile early and doesn't use the leftover time on another pile that hour). Find the smallest possible speed k that still lets her finish everything within h hours.

examples.explanation: If Koko eats 4 bananas per hour, she needs 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours total, exactly meeting the deadline. Any slower speed would take too long.
With only 5 hours and 5 piles, Koko can eat at most one pile per hour, so she must eat fast enough to finish the biggest pile (30 bananas) in a single hour.

constraints: 1 <= piles.length <= 10^4 (there are 1 to 10,000 piles)
piles.length <= h <= 10^9 (hours available is at least the number of piles, since she needs at least 1 hour per pile)
1 <= piles[i] <= 10^9 (each pile can have up to a billion bananas)
hints: Binary search the eating speed k in the range from 1 to the maximum pile size.
For each candidate speed k, calculate total hours needed as the sum of ceil(pile / k) across all piles.
relatedProblems: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
Minimum Speed to Arrive on Time
followUp: Can you turn your 'is this speed fast enough' check into a reusable helper function/template for similar problems?

testCases.note: Normal case - deadline is somewhat tight, requiring a moderate eating speed.
Edge case - hours exactly equal the number of piles, forcing maximum possible speed.
Edge case - single very large pile, testing that your code handles big numbers efficiently.
Edge case - smallest possible input, one pile with one banana and one hour.
Edge case - huge number of hours available compared to bananas, so the slowest possible speed (1) is enough.

title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
description: You have a list of package weights that must be shipped in their given order (you cannot reorder them), and you have exactly d days to ship everything. Each day, you load the ship with as many packages as fit without exceeding its weight capacity, then move to the next day. Find the smallest ship capacity that still allows you to finish shipping within d days.

examples.explanation: With a ship capacity of 15, you can group the packages into 5 days worth of shipments without exceeding 15 on any day, and no smaller capacity would work within 5 days.
A capacity of 6 lets you split the packages into exactly 3 days worth of shipments.

constraints: 1 <= days <= weights.length <= 5 * 10^4 (there are between 1 and 50,000 packages, and days is at most the number of packages)
1 <= weights[i] <= 500 (each package weighs between 1 and 500)
hints: Binary search the capacity between max(weights) and the sum of all weights.
For each candidate capacity, greedily simulate how many days it would actually take to ship everything.

youtubeVideos.title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days - NeetCode

followUp: What would change if the packages could be reordered before shipping, instead of keeping their original order?

testCases.note: Normal case - moderate number of packages and days.
Normal case - smaller list with a tighter day constraint.
Edge case - days is close to the number of packages, so capacity must be at least the heaviest single package.
Edge case - only one package and one day, so capacity must equal that package's weight.
Edge case - one package per day exactly, testing the minimum possible capacity boundary.

title: Find Right Interval
description: You are given a list of intervals (each interval has a start and end point). For every interval, you need to find another interval whose start point is the smallest value that is still greater than or equal to the current interval's end point - basically, the 'closest interval that starts right after this one ends'. If no such interval exists, return -1 for that one.

examples.explanation: For interval [3,4] (ends at 4), no interval starts at 4 or later, so the answer is -1. For [2,3] (ends at 3), interval [3,4] at original index 0 starts exactly at 3. For [1,2] (ends at 2), interval [2,3] at original index 1 starts exactly at 2.
Only the middle interval [2,3] (ends at 3) has a matching interval that starts at or after 3 - which is [3,4] at index 2. The others have no valid match.

constraints: 1 <= intervals.length <= 2 * 10^4 (between 1 and 20,000 intervals)
intervals[i].length == 2 (each interval has exactly a start and an end)
-10^6 <= starti <= endi <= 10^6 (start is always less than or equal to end)
Every interval's start point is unique (no two intervals start at the exact same point)
hints: Sort the intervals' start points while remembering each one's original index.
For each interval's end point, binary search for the smallest start point that is >= that end point.
relatedProblems: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target
followUp: Could you solve this using a sorted map / tree-based structure instead of sorting an array?

testCases.note: Normal case - a chain of intervals where most have a valid right match.
Normal case - only one interval has a valid match, others return -1.
Edge case - only one interval, and it matches itself since its own start equals its own end.
Edge case - no interval has a match for the last one, so it returns -1.
Edge case - a single interval where the start is far below the end, but it still matches itself.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description: You are given a grid (matrix) of numbers with a special property: each row is sorted left-to-right, and the first number of every row is bigger than the last number of the row above it. Determine whether a given target value exists anywhere in the matrix.

examples.explanation: If you read the matrix row by row, it reads 1,3,5,7,10,11,16,20,23,30,34,60 - fully sorted. The value 3 is present, so we return true.
13 does not appear anywhere in the grid, so we return false.

constraints: m == matrix.length (number of rows)
n == matrix[i].length (number of columns)
1 <= m, n <= 100 (grid can be up to 100 rows and 100 columns)
-10^4 <= matrix[i][j], target <= 10^4
hints: Treat the 2D matrix as one long, flattened, sorted 1D array of length m * n.
Convert a flat 'mid' index back to a row and column using row = mid / n and column = mid % n.
relatedProblems: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix
followUp: How would your approach need to change if the matrix were sorted differently, like in Search a 2D Matrix II?

testCases.note: Normal case - target exists in the first row.
Normal case - target does not exist anywhere.
Edge case - smallest possible matrix (a single cell) that matches the target.
Edge case - smallest possible matrix (a single cell) that does not match.
Edge case - target is the very last (largest) value in the entire matrix.

title: Minimum Speed to Arrive on Time
description: You need to catch several train rides back-to-back to reach a destination by a certain deadline (given in hours, which can include a decimal like 2.5). For every ride except the very last one, if you don't finish exactly at a whole-hour mark, you must wait until the next whole hour before boarding the next train (so those times get rounded up). Only the very last ride's time counts exactly, with no rounding. Find the smallest whole-number train speed that still gets you there on time.

examples.explanation: At a speed of 1, the first two rides take 1 hour and 3 hours (both round up to whole hours), and the last ride takes exactly 2 hours without rounding, for a total of exactly 6 hours - just barely making the deadline.
The deadline is much tighter here (2.7 hours), so a faster speed of 3 is required to squeeze in all three rides in time.

constraints: n == dist.length (number of train rides)
1 <= dist[i] <= 10^5 (distance of each ride)
1 <= hour <= 10^9 (deadline in hours, can be very large)
The deadline (hour) will have at most 2 digits after the decimal point
hints: Binary search the speed in the range from 1 to 10^7.
For every ride except the last one, round the travel time up to the next whole hour; for the very last ride, use the exact (non-rounded) division.

youtubeVideos.title: Minimum Speed to Arrive on Time - LeetCode 1870

relatedProblems: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
followUp: What would change in your approach if speeds were allowed to be decimal numbers instead of only whole numbers?

testCases.note: Normal case - deadline is exactly achievable at the slowest possible speed.
Normal case - a tight deadline requiring a faster speed.
Edge case - deadline is barely more than the number of rides, forcing the maximum possible speed.
Edge case - even the slowest speed easily meets a generous deadline.
Edge case - it's mathematically impossible to make it on time even at maximum speed, so the answer is -1 (there's not enough hours for even 3 separate one-hour-rounded rides).

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
description: This is the same challenge as 'Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array', except now the array is allowed to contain duplicate numbers. Find the smallest number in the rotated array.

examples.explanation: This array actually was not rotated at all (or rotated a full circle back to itself), so it's already sorted, and the minimum is simply the first value, 1.
Even though there are repeated 2's making parts of the search ambiguous, the true minimum value in the array is 0.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 5000 (array has 1 to 5000 numbers)

title: Split Array Largest Sum
description: You are given an array of numbers and an integer k. You must split the array into exactly k pieces (each piece must be a continuous chunk, and no piece can be empty), and you want to choose the split points so that the 'largest sum among all the pieces' is as small as possible - basically, spreading the numbers out as evenly as possible across the k groups.

examples.explanation: Splitting into [7,2,5] (sum 14) and [10,8] (sum 18), the largest of the two sums is 18. No other way to split into exactly 2 pieces gives a smaller 'largest sum'.
Splitting into [1,2,3] (sum 6) and [4,5] (sum 9), the largest sum is 9, which is the smallest possible largest-sum for 2 pieces.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000 (array has 1 to 1000 numbers)
0 <= nums[i] <= 10^6 (each number is between 0 and 1,000,000)
1 <= k <= min(50, nums.length) (you can split into at most 50 pieces, and never more pieces than there are numbers)
hints: Binary search the answer between the largest single number in the array and the sum of the whole array.
For each candidate maximum sum, greedily count how many pieces you'd actually need to stay under that maximum.
relatedProblems: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
followUp: Can you also solve this using dynamic programming, and how does its speed compare to the binary search approach?

Normal case - a simple increasing sequence split into two groups.

Edge case - single element and only one piece required, so the answer is just that one number.
Edge case - moderately sized array being split into many small pieces, testing tighter grouping logic.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: You are given two separate sorted arrays, and you need to find the median (the middle value) if you imagine merging them into one big sorted array - but you must do this in O(log(min(m, n))) time, without actually merging them.

examples.explanation: If you merged both arrays together, you'd get [1, 2, 3]. Since there are 3 total numbers (odd count), the median is simply the middle one, 2.
Merged together, you'd get [1, 2, 3, 4]. Since there are 4 total numbers (even count), the median is the average of the two middle values: (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

constraints: nums1.length == m
nums2.length == n
0 <= m <= 1000 (first array can be empty, up to 1000 elements)
0 <= n <= 1000 (second array can be empty, up to 1000 elements)
1 <= m + n <= 2000 (both arrays together must have at least 1 element total)
hints: Binary search for the correct partition point in whichever array is smaller, to keep things efficient.
Compare the values at the boundary of each partition (maxLeft vs minRight) to check whether your current split is valid or needs adjusting.

title: Find in Mountain Array
description: You are given a 'mountain array' (numbers that rise to one peak and then fall), but you can't view it directly - you can only access it through a special interactive function called mountainArr.get(index), and every call to that function costs you, so you want to minimize how many times you call it. Your goal: find the smallest index where a target value appears, or return -1 if it's not present anywhere.

examples.explanation: The value 3 actually appears twice in this array - once at index 2 (on the way up the mountain) and once at index 5 (on the way down). Since we want the smallest index, we return 2.
The value 3 does not appear anywhere in this mountain array, so we return -1.

constraints: 3 <= mountain_arr.length() <= 10^4 (the mountain has at least 3 elements, since it needs an up-slope, peak, and down-slope)
0 <= target <= 10^9
0 <= mountain_arr.get(index) <= 10^9
You should try to minimize the number of calls to mountainArr.get(), since each call is treated as costly
hints: First, binary search to find the peak's index using the local slope comparison trick (compare a value to its neighbor).
Then binary search the ascending half for the target, and only if it's not found there, binary search the descending half too.
relatedProblems: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
followUp: How would you further minimize the total number of API queries used across all three binary searches combined?

testCases.note: Normal case - target appears on both slopes; smallest index (ascending side) is returned.
Normal case - target does not exist anywhere in the mountain.
Edge case - smallest possible mountain array (3 elements), target is exactly the peak.
Edge case - target is at the very first index of a purely ascending mountain (peak is at the end).
